meta.audience: All the Lamanites under the king's proclamation
meta.unit: The sons of Mosiah among the Lamanites (Alma 17–26)
principles: Law that clears the way for the word
A new name taken on purpose

world_behind.title: The decree lists the abuses it forbids
world_behind.text: Verse 2 names binding, prison, spitting, striking, expulsion from synagogues, scourging, and stoning. The specificity tells the reader what the missionaries had already been meeting.

world_behind.title: Free access is granted to three kinds of building
world_behind.text: Verse 2 gives the brethren their houses, their temples, and their sanctuaries. The Lamanites had temples, and the record mentions the fact in passing while listing something else.

world_behind.title: The king's stated purpose is civic
world_behind.text: Verse 3 wants his people convinced that the traditions were wicked, that they are all brethren, and that murder, plunder, theft, and adultery are out. He is legislating a moral code alongside a religious opening.

world_behind.title: Aaron builds an organization
world_behind.text: Verse 4 has him going city to city and house of worship to house of worship, establishing churches and consecrating priests and teachers. The mission stops being itinerant and becomes local leadership.

world_behind.title: The roll of cities is a document
world_behind.text: Verses 9 through 13 read like a list copied from somewhere: Ishmael, Middoni, Nephi, Shilom, Shemlon, Lemuel, Shimnilom. Mormon says in verse 15 that he has named them all.

world_behind.title: Amulon's people and the Amalekites hold out entirely
world_behind.text: Verse 14 records one Amalekite convert and no Amulonites, and says they hardened the Lamanites around them. The dissenters stay the wall.

world_behind.title: The name is chosen by committee
world_behind.text: Verse 16 has the king consult Aaron and many of their priests about what to call themselves. The record shows a deliberate act of naming, taken so the converts could be told apart from their own nation.

words.text: To whip, as a legal or mob punishment. Treated at Jacob 3:3. The decree forbids it explicitly. The record uses the word eleven times and the King James Bible twelve, and Christ warns his own missionaries in Matthew 10 that they will be scourged in synagogues. A Lamanite king outlaws in advance what the apostles were promised.

Anything set in the way. The word occurs once in scripture. The king sends his proclamation so that the word of God might have no obstruction, which frames the decree as clearing a road instead of compelling belief.

Setting apart for sacred service. This participle appears once in the record. It names what Aaron did in every city: leaving behind priests and teachers who belonged to the place, so that the work continued after he walked out.

A Lamanite land near the city of Nephi. It appears six times, five of them in Mosiah, where it is the staging ground for the armies that attacked Noah and the place the daughters of the Lamanites were taken from. Alma 23 lists it among the converted.

The name the converts chose for themselves. It occurs once in this form and is never explained. Whatever the elements mean, the effect is plain: they stopped being called Lamanites and took a name built out of Nephi and Lehi.

Diligent in work. The record uses it four times, always of a people building something after a break with their past: Nephi's colony in 2 Nephi 5, Alma's people at Helam, the Jaredites under Lib. Mormon applies the same word to a nation that has just put down its weapons.

phrases.term: Nor either of their brethren who should go forth preaching the word of God
phrases.text: The protection is written to cover men the king has never met. He extends it to any future missionary in any part of his land. The decree is drafted as a standing policy instead of a personal favor.

phrases.term: Neither should they spit upon them, nor smite them, nor cast them out of their synagogues
phrases.text: A list of specific indignities, banned one at a time. Every item is something someone had done. The verse is a record of persecution written in the form of a law against it.

phrases.term: That the word of God might have no obstruction
phrases.text: The king's own statement of what he is doing. He clears the road and leaves the walking to his people. Nothing in the decree requires anyone to believe.

phrases.term: That they might be convinced that they were all brethren
phrases.text: Six centuries of blood feud, addressed in a clause. The king wants his people persuaded of kinship with the Nephites, which is the practical content of what Aaron taught him about the fall and the atonement.

phrases.term: Thousands were brought to believe in the traditions of the Nephites
phrases.text: Mormon names the change in the terms the quarrel used. Lamanite identity was built on the wickedness of Nephite traditions, and the converts crossed over on exactly that ground.
Mormon swears to it twice in one verse, as sure as the Lord liveth. The claim covers every Lamanite converted in this mission. He is writing centuries later with the whole outcome in front of him.

phrases.term: They did lay down the weapons of their rebellion
phrases.text: The first statement of the act that defines this people. Mormon calls the weapons theirs by rebellion, so putting them down is described as the end of a war against God before it is a policy toward men.

phrases.term: The Amalekites were not converted, save only one
phrases.text: One man out of a whole dissenting nation. Mormon counts him. The record keeps the exception in the sentence that reports the failure.

phrases.term: That thereby they might be distinguished from their brethren
phrases.text: The converts ask for a name because they need to be told apart. The request is practical and it is also a separation from their own people, made deliberately and with the king's participation.

phrases.term: They did open a correspondence with them
phrases.text: Letters between Lamanites and Nephites. The word appears four times in this record, three of them in these chapters, and it marks the moment two nations start writing to each other after six hundred years of raiding.

verses.label: v. 1–2
verses.title: A decree written entirely as a list of prohibitions
verses.text: The record gives the proclamation by naming seven things that may not be done: they should not "lay their hands on them to bind them, or to cast them into prison; neither should they spit upon them, nor smite them, nor cast them out of their synagogues, nor scourge them; neither should they cast stones at them." Only at the end does one positive clause arrive, "but that they should have free access to their houses, and also their temples, and their sanctuaries." The seven forbidden acts are also, item for item, what happened to Alma and Amulek nine chapters earlier at Ammonihah.

verses.label: v. 6
verses.title: A claim made twice over, with an oath on each side
verses.text: The record does not simply report that the converts held. It underwrites the statement: "as sure as the Lord liveth, so sure as many as believed... yea, I say unto you, as the Lord liveth, as many of the Lamanites as believed in their preaching, and were converted unto the Lord, never did fall away." The formula appears at both ends of the verse, and the claim between them is absolute rather than statistical. The writer takes the oath here; no character does.

verses.label: v. 8–13
verses.title: Seven places, listed one to a verse
verses.text: Verse 8 announces a list, "Now, these are they who were converted unto the Lord," and the next five verses supply it in an almost bare form: the land of Ishmael, the land of Middoni, the city of Nephi, and then four in a single verse, "the land of Shilom, and who were in the land of Shemlon, and in the city of Lemuel, and in the city of Shimnilom." No number of converts is given for any of them and no event is attached. The list is a register of places, and the chapter is willing to spend a quarter of its verses on it.

verses.label: v. 14
verses.title: An exception counted to one
verses.text: Between the two closures sits the qualification: "the Amalekites were not converted, save only one; neither were any of the Amulonites; but they did harden their hearts." The record has just declined to number the thousands who believed, and here it counts a single man on the other side. The same two groups are singled out again at Alma 24:29, where the record notes that none of the converts came from them, so the exception is tracked across two chapters.

chapter.title: The law clears the way and stops there
chapter.text: Every clause of the decree removes an obstacle. Nothing in it compels belief or penalizes unbelief, and Mormon puts the king's own purpose in verse 3 so the reader can check.

chapter.title: Persecution is documented by the ban on it
chapter.text: The catalogue in verse 2 is the fullest list in the record of what happened to these missionaries, and it survives only because someone made it illegal.

chapter.title: Aaron leaves people behind
chapter.text: Verse 4 reports the method as a circuit with an appointment at every stop, "from city to city, and from one house of worship to another, establishing churches, and consecrating priests and teachers throughout the land." Verse 5 gives the result in two figures, "thousands were brought to the knowledge of the Lord," and specifies what they were taught, "the records and prophecies which were handed down." Verses 9 through 13 then name seven cities and lands and add a count, "the people of Ammon, and they were called thus ever after." The chapter reports a structure being left behind rather than a sermon being remembered.

chapter.title: Mormon puts his own oath behind the perseverance
chapter.text: He says as sure as the Lord liveth twice in verse 6. That is the strongest endorsement he gives any group in the record, and Alma 24 shows what it cost them.

chapter.title: Laying down weapons is named before it is explained
chapter.text: Verse 7 states the act; Alma 24 gives the covenant and the burial. Here it arrives as a simple consequence of no longer fighting God.

chapter.title: The dissenters are the immovable ones
chapter.text: One convert among the Amalekites, none among the Amulonites. Men who had held the record and left it prove harder than a nation that never had it.

chapter.title: A people renames itself out of the enemy's ancestors
chapter.text: Nephi and Lehi are in the name they choose, and the record notes only that Lamanite is no longer used of them. Identity changes by decision and consultation, in public.

chapter.title: The chapter ends with mail
chapter.text: After the decree, the churches, the roll, and the new name, the last thing Mormon records is that two nations started writing to each other. That correspondence is what makes Alma 27 possible.

applications.title: Publish the protection in specific terms
applications.text: The decree does not say to be tolerant. It lists the forbidden acts: not to bind them, not to cast them into prison, not to spit upon them, not to smite them, not to cast them out of their synagogues. A protection that names the behaviours is enforceable in a way that a sentiment is not.

applications.title: Leave a structure behind, not a visit
applications.text: He worked city by city and house of worship by house of worship, ordaining as he went, "from city to city, and from one house of worship to another, establishing churches, and consecrating priests and teachers." What made the difference was the ordination; the sermon did not.

applications.title: Teach the records, not only the message
applications.text: The converts "were taught the records and prophecies which were handed down even to the present time." Handing over the material people can read for themselves outlasts what they heard you say.

applications.title: Notice a conversion that holds
applications.text: The record makes a claim it makes almost nowhere else, that as many as believed "never did fall away." When something works, it is worth asking what was different about how it was done rather than only celebrating that it worked.

applications.title: Lay down the weapons of the rebellion, whatever they are
applications.text: The phrase is not only about arms, "they did lay down the weapons of their rebellion, that they did not fight against God any more, neither against any of their brethren." Name yours; some of them are habits rather than objects.

applications.title: Record the exceptions honestly
applications.text: The chapter names who did not convert, "the Amalekites were not converted, save only one; neither were any of the Amulonites." An account of a success that reports its own limits is worth more than one that does not.

applications.title: Take a new name when the old one is a description
applications.text: They called themselves Anti-Nephi-Lehies and "were no more called Lamanites." A change deep enough to need a different word for it is worth marking with one.

applications.title: Expect the change to be visible in the ordinary week
applications.text: The evidence given is industriousness, friendliness with the Nephites, and an opened correspondence. None of it is devotional. Ask what has changed in your working life since whatever you count as your turning.

questions.text: What indignity have I treated as normal because nobody ever forbade it?
What obstruction could I remove for someone this week?
Who is carrying on something I started, and did I actually hand it to them?
What in my life have I let fall away that I once knew was true?
What weapon am I still holding, and what am I calling it?
Where have I hardened myself while people around me changed?
If I had to take a name that showed what I have become, what would it be built out of?
